extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary) and patent practitioners/applicants working on U.S. design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and responding to restriction requirements and double-patenting issues in U.S. design patent practice, including when multiple embodiments may be grouped, when restriction is required, standards for statutory and nonstatutory double patenting, and priority/terminal-disclaimer procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentably distinct embodiments cannot be included in same design application
rubrics_metrics.description: Embodiments that are patentably distinct from one another do not constitute a single inventive concept and thus may not be included in the same design application. Multiple embodiments of a single inventive concept may be included only if they are patentably indistinct. (Cites: In re Rubinfield; In re Platner.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If embodiments have overall appearances that are not basically the same, or if differences are not minor/patentably indistinct or are not shown to be obvious over analogous prior art, they must be treated as distinct. Designs covering segregable, patentably distinct parts require separate patents; combination vs subcombination subject matter, if patentably distinct, must be supported by separate claims. Examiner should group obvious variations together as a single inventive concept; otherwise restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction requirement and mandatory election of a single group
rubrics_metrics.description: When restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121, applicant must elect a single group for prosecution on the merits; a reply not including an election of a single group will be held nonresponsive. Examiner may request cancellation of drawing figures and descriptions directed to nonelected groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs and bracketed language are used to notify applicant. If election is made without traverse, nonelected groups should be canceled. If the requirement is maintained and not complied with, action on the merits is deferred pending compliance. See 37 CFR 1.143, 1.142(b), and 1.144 for procedural handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to traverse restriction requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant traverses the restriction on grounds that groups are not patentably distinct, applicant must present evidence or identify evidence of record showing the groups to be obvious variations of one another; traversal alone without explanation is treated as an election without traverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant should supply factual showings demonstrating obvious variation. If groups are later determined not to be patentably distinct and remain in the application, any rejection over prior art of one group will apply to all. If traversal points out alleged errors, the examiner must reevaluate; if maintained, restriction must be repeated and made final and arguments answered. See MPEP §803, §818.01(c), form paragraph 8.25.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping rule for multiple embodiments within a group
rubrics_metrics.description: Embodiments included in a single group are considered by the examiner to be obvious variations of one another within the group and therefore patentably indistinct, comprising a single inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple embodiments are grouped, examiner should ensure that the variations are indeed obvious to a designer of ordinary skill; explanatory paragraphs should describe differences among embodiments (e.g., which figures relate to which parts). Examiner notes provide where to insert explanations and embodiments in form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone provisional elections must be affirmed in reply
rubrics_metrics.description: When a provisional election is made during a telephone discussion, applicant must affirm the election in the reply to the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provisional election statement made during telephone contact should be renewed in the formal reply; form paragraphs identify placeholders for dates and provisional election details. Failure to affirm may require contacting applicant or using form paragraph 8.03 to advise options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifying statement for common embodiment included in more than one group
rubrics_metrics.description: If a common embodiment is included in more than one group because it is patentably indistinct from other embodiments, applicant is advised that the common embodiment should not be included in any continuing application if elected in this application to avoid double patenting under 35 U.S.C. 171.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual provides form language to notify applicant that inclusion of a common embodiment in continuing filings may lead to double patenting problems. Applicant should be cautioned to avoid including a common embodiment in later applications once elected in the parent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory (“same invention”) double patenting (35 U.S.C. 171) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A statutory same-invention double patenting rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 applies where identical designs with identical scope are claimed twice (design-design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejection prevents issuance of a second patent for a design already patented. A terminal disclaimer may not be used to overcome a 'same invention' type double patenting rejection. Use form paragraph 15.23.02 following such rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting doctrine and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstatutory double patenting is a judicially created doctrine used to prevent unjustified timewise extension of patent rights and to avoid multiple suits by different assignees over patentably indistinct variations of the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonstatutory rejections are grounded in public policy and can be based on anticipation, one-way obviousness, or two-way obviousness style analyses. Case law references (e.g., In re Goodman; In re Van Ornum) are cited. Charts in MPEP §804 outline procedures for handling double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting — overall appearance comparison rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine nonstatutory double patenting, the examiner must compare the overall appearance of the claimed design in the application with the overall appearance of the claimed design in the conflicting application or patent; the claim must be considered as a whole rather than by isolated elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike anticipation/obviousness where elements may be considered individually, the nonstatutory double patenting analysis focuses on overall design characteristics. If overall appearances are basically the same and differences are insufficient to patentably distinguish (de minimis or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill), nonstatutory double patenting may be appropriate. See MPEP §804 (II.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part test for nonstatutory double patenting when scope differs
rubrics_metrics.description: When designs have differing scope, a nonstatutory double patenting rejection is appropriate if: (A) the difference in scope is minor and patentably indistinct; (B) allowance of the later claim would extend patent protection fully disclosed/covered by the earlier claim; and (C) no terminal disclaimer has been filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This often arises between a combination (narrow claim) and a subcombination/element (broad claim). Examiner must determine whether the narrower subject matter is fully disclosed and covered by the broader claim of the reference. If the broader claim does not disclose the narrower claim, NSDP rejection is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer use and requirements to overcome NSDP
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) may be used to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection provided the conflicting application or patent is commonly owned; the terminal disclaimer must be signed per 37 CFR 1.321(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a terminal disclaimer alone is not a complete reply to an NSDP rejection — it must be accompanied by a reply requesting reconsideration (see 37 CFR 1.111(a), 1.113(c) for replies to non-final/final actions). USPTO provides eTerminal Disclaimer forms; an eTerminal Disclaimer that meets requirements is auto-processed. Examiner notes and web links provided for forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional double patenting rejections and conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional double patenting rejection (statutory or nonstatutory) applied between copending applications will be converted into a double patenting rejection when the first application publishes or issues as a patent; provisional rejections are appropriate when conflicting claims have not yet been patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple applications conflict and one is allowed, remaining applications should be cross-rejected against others and the allowed application. Examiners should consult MPEP §1490 VI.D for withdrawing provisional rejections when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-way vs two-way distinctness determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Design-design nonstatutory double patenting rejections do not always have to be made in both conflicting applications; if the rejection is only appropriate in one direction, it is proper to reject only one application. However, design-utility situations require a two-way distinctness determination for the rejection to be proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should follow criteria in MPEP §804 II.B.4 and II.B.5 to decide whether one-way or two-way determinations are needed. Consider common inventorship, common applicant, or ownership and whether claims create a one-way rather than mutual indistinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority for design applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 172 (six-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of priority to an earlier foreign filing for designs is six months (35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d), 172). Design applications may not claim the benefit of a provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain benefit of an earlier foreign filing date, the U.S. application must be filed within six months of the earliest foreign filing for the same design. If filed within two months after the six-month period and the delay was unintentional, applicant may file a petition under 37 CFR 1.55(c) to restore priority. If a certified copy is filed but the priority claim not properly made, the claim must be presented during pendency (or via petition under 37 CFR 1.55(e)). See MPEP §213-216 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for petition to restore right of priority (37 CFR 1.55(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to restore priority must include: (1) the priority claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d), 386(a) or (b) in an application data sheet identifying the foreign application number/country/date; (2) the petition fee per 37 CFR 1.17(m); and (3) a statement that the delay in filing within the six-month period was unintentional. The petition must be filed in the subsequent application (or earliest nonprovisional claiming benefit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director may require additional information where question exists whether delay was unintentional. Address for filing and further procedural instructions are provided in the manual. If the claim for priority is filed after the issue fee is paid, the patent will not include the priority claim unless corrected by certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323.
